title: Jesus Owono given 12-match ban for collision with Jesus de Miguel that led to striker’s death

that led to striker’s death
 De Miguel died in hospital on November 3 following a collision with Owono during a match between Tenerife and Andorra the previous night. Walter Cunha/NurPhoto via Getty Images 
 By Mario Cortegana Nov. 13, 2026 Updated 6:01 pm EST Share article 119 Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono has been given a 12-match suspension after the collision with Jesus de Miguel that led to the Tenerife striker’s death.
 De Miguel died in hospital on November 3 following a collision with Owono during a Spanish second-division match the previous night.
 Spanish police told The Athletic an investigation into De Miguel’s death has been opened, in co-ordination with judicial authorities in Tenerife, as is required for any death without a clear natural cause.
 Advertisement
 The collision between De Miguel, 30, and Owono, 25, resulted in the Segunda Division fixture being abandoned in the sixth minute of second-half stoppage time.
 Teams across Europe held a minute of silence for De Miguel (Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty Images) Owono had come out to challenge for a high ball when he collided with De Miguel. The Andorra goalkeeper was shown a straight red card for the challenge. He, alongside his team-mates and opponents, rushed to check on De Miguel, who appeared motionless and was taken to hospital.
 Referee Manuel Angel Perez Hernandez’s match report explained he gave Owono a red card because the Equatorial Guinea international had made “a reckless challenge with his leg raised, using excessive force against an opponent whilst the ball was in play”.
 The disciplinary committee of the Spanish Football Federation has now decided to ban Owono for 12 games, the longest possible suspension under article 102 of their regulations.
 Owono was also fined €600 (£500; $661) for the incident under article 52 of the disciplinary regulations, while Andorra were fined €2,400.
 In his first public comment since the incident, published on Andorra’s social media earlier this month, Owono said he has experienced the “hardest days of my life” and expressed his “immense grief”.
 “These have been the hardest days of my life,” he wrote. “I’m struggling to find the words and find it very difficult to come to terms with anything that has happened. I feel immense grief at the loss of Jesus.
 “My thoughts are with him, his family and everyone who loved him. I know there will be many matters to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, quite honestly, I cannot think of anything other than Jesus and the grief we are experiencing. Rest in peace, Jesus.”
 How has the Spanish FA approached this? 
 The Spanish FA’s disciplinary committee has responsibility for issuing sanctions to players. In most red card cases, the referee’s description in their match report dictates which particular section of the disciplinary regulations is applied when deciding suspensions.
 Advertisement
 Because, as noted in referee Perez Hernandez’s report, the ball was being contested at the time of Owono’s challenge on De Miguel, the Spanish FA’s disciplinary committee applied article 102 of its disciplinary code. This relates to violent conduct during play resulting in serious harm or injury, and can carry a suspension of between four and 12 matches.

 Jesus de Miguel’s tragic death: How Spanish football was struck by sorrow
 The 30-year-old CD Tenerife striker died on Tuesday following a horrific collision with an opposition goalkeeper the day before
 Perez Hernandez’s match report also explained why the match was abandoned shortly after the collision between Owono and De Miguel.
 “Given the seriousness of the situation and as there was no sign of improvement in the player’s condition, we withdrew to the changing rooms,” it read.
 “Once we had met with the captains and team representatives from both sides, we were informed that they were not in the right frame of mind to continue the match. It was therefore decided to call off the match by mutual agreement between all parties.”
 Are legal authorities investigating? 
 Following De Miguel’s death, the Canary Islands High Court of Justice (TSJC) said a judicial investigation was automatically opened, as is standard procedure in any case of a non-natural death, whether caused by an accident or other circumstances.
 The investigation is being handled by Court No. 2 of the Investigative Section of the Court of First Instance in Santa Cruz de Tenerife, which was on duty when the incident occurred on Monday. The TSJC said the police are currently handling the investigation and will submit their report to the court once their inquiries are complete.
 National Police sources also confirmed that an investigation was under way in coordination with the judicial authorities. However, the opening of a judicial investigation does not necessarily mean criminal proceedings will follow.
 Speaking on Tuesday, Santa Cruz de Tenerife’s chief prosecutor, Jose Luis Sanchez-Jauregui, told news agency EFE it was very unlikely that a criminal case would be initiated. A Canary Islands prosecutorial source echoed this when consulted by The Athletic .
 Spanish media reports have said that, in addition to seeking to establish the exact cause of death, the investigation has been examining how De Miguel was treated by medical services after the collision with Owono, though there has been no suggestion that the medical care was substandard.
